extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of advertising history; historians and advertising practitioners interested in early practices
extracted.subtask_description: A historical survey of advertising methods from medieval vocal cries and church-door notices through broadsides, shop-window placards, processions, bellmen, and the earliest newspaper advertisements. Emphasises how goods and events were publicised and the conventional forms used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tavern-cries / vocal proclamation of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mine host proclaiming in the street that he has 'good, cool, and new wine... bread and meat, and wine and fish: within is a good place to spend your money; within is accommodation for all kind of people; here is good lodging.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vocal, street-calls listing specific goods and inviting trade — illustrated by examples from 'Trois Aveugles de Compiegne' and 'Debats et facd'tieuses rencontres.' Used as immediate, attention-getting advertisement by innkeepers and taverners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written handbills and broadsides affixed in public places
rubrics_metrics.description: Written handbills were affixed in public places; with the invention of printing this was applied to multiply advertisements (early printed poster by Caxton, circa 1480).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posters/broadsides were produced and posted in frequented public spots (church doors, market places). Example: Caxton's 'Pyes of Salisbury use' broadside (five by seven inches) with location and sale notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin notices with 'If anybody' / 'Si quis' formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements almost invariably commenced with the words 'If anybody,' or in Latin 'Si quis'; from these words they obtained their name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This opening formula was a conventional attention device and persisted into later ecclesiastical notices (the 'siquis' door). Ben Jonson and Caxton use the same concluding formula 'siet quceso^' pleading with the reader not to tear the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affix notices near churches / use of church doors (St Paul's, London Stone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handbills were posted in the most frequented parts of towns, preferably near churches; in London the middle aisle of St Paul's was a principal place for affixing siquis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church doors served as public notice-boards for employment, ecclesiastical applications, auctions, and miscellaneous classifieds — a proto-classifieds column of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use printed book-notices and shop-window advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: The University compelled booksellers to advertise new manuscripts in shop windows; after printing booksellers proclaimed cheapness and new works in their shops or in the books themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booksellers posted notices in shop windows or fixed placards in cleft sticks; Ben Jonson mentions/book-epigram discouraging use of posts or walls for advertising small leaflets, indicating common shop-front advertising practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise cheapness/low price as a selling point
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers and booksellers extolled the low price of their works inside the book (examples: Ulric Gering, Berthold Remboldt, Thielman Kerver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statements about cheapness (sometimes in Latin distichs) were used to allay purchaser fears and encourage sales; sometimes advertised as 'sold for a very small sum' or 'to be had for a trifling sum.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scholarly endorsements / 'puff direct' by editors or scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers sometimes had a book puffed on account of its cheapness by editors or scholars of known eminence who address the public on behalf of the printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 'Les Opuscules du Docteur Almain' (1518) a dignified member of the University praises the publishers; this is recorded as the earliest instance of direct puffing discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of processions, animals, banners and noisy instruments to announce shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements of shows (bearbaitings, equestrian circuses) were given by bills and processions — the bears led about the town preceded by a flag and noisy instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical spectacle (parading animals, bagpipes, drums) functioned as mobile advertising to draw crowds and publicise time/place of entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promenade of combatants and noisy pre-announcements for trials of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials of skill were announced by combatants promenading the streets divested of upper garments, with sleeves tucked up, sword or cudgel in hand, and preceded by a drum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public display of participants and instruments served as a visual-auditory advertisement to stimulate interest and attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a bellman / town crier for community notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The bellman or town crier proclaimed matters for the community: lost and found, sales by public auction or private contract, weddings, christenings, funerals, and other notifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vocal announcements by an official cryer, often accompanied by printed 'Cries of London' prints; continued use in provincial towns into modern times as an effective local publicity mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprentice/shop-door calling as continuous oral advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every shopkeeper kept an apprentice at his door to attract the attention of passers-by with continuous 'What do you lack, master?' followed by enumeration of wares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live, repeated oral listing of goods to passing foot traffic served as an immediate sales prompt — a street-level attention-getting technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early newspaper paragraphs and miscellaneous advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: The earliest newspaper paragraphs approaching advertisements appeared in late 16th/early 17th century newsbooks and periodicals (German, Dutch, French); they ranged from book notices to auctions of prize goods and inauguration notices for schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers began to include distinct advertisements (in separate type) such as auctions of sugar/tobacco/logwood, sales of museum collections, announcements of schools and published treatises; examples from 1581, 1626, 1633, 1634.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puff-pars and self-promotional paragraphs in newsbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Early newspaper-style advertisements often resembled 'puff pars' — promotional notices praising a work and urging immediate purchase (e.g., a German newsbook urging readers to 'buy the book at once').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These short promotional blurbs acted as paid or self-promotional copy, similar to later book adverts, and were sometimes printed in different type to distinguish them from news.

rubrics_metrics.name: List specific sale details (goods, date, place) for auctions and public sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements for sales and auctions listed the items (sugar, ivory, pepper, tobacco, logwood), the form of sale (public auction or private contract), and the date/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing precise, actionable details (what is for sale, how, where, when) is illustrated by Dutch and other early newspaper ads and was essential to convert interest into attendance/purchase.
